title: The Lotus Opens
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 21 of 40
content:
The first morning after I began helping, Iroh gave me a key and rules in elegant handwriting. The tea shop before opening carried the smell of brass keys, and Ba Sing Se woke around us in cart wheels, shutters, and distant voices. I had learned that Iroh's shop was never merely a shop. It was refuge, theater, kitchen, meeting place, and sometimes a place where an old general pretended he had no past. I had also learned that pretending was different from lying. Today I wanted to know which one he asked of me.

The plan was to learn whether my place was temporary labor or a life he would make room for. Iroh made difficult things sound easy because he believed they deserved a calm beginning. He poured tea, straightened a chair, and turned a practical task into a small ceremony. I let him do it for a while. Then I asked what part belonged to him and what part belonged to me. His eyebrows lifted. I had learned not to mistake that expression for surprise. Often it meant he was delighted to be challenged.

The complication was already there: the key fit the door, but Iroh still treated asking me to stay as an imposition. It arrived without announcing itself, as important things often did. Iroh's posture changed first. The hand holding the cup became still. His smile remained, but it was no longer doing all the work. He measured tea by instinct, corrected my grip only after asking, and called the squeaky hinge loyal. I watched the old power move beneath the surface and waited for him to decide what kind of man he wanted to be in front of me.

I did not wait passively. I asked for a chair at the counter and a voice in decisions affecting us. Iroh had been trained to notice what people needed before they said it. I wanted to be more difficult than that. I wanted to say what I needed aloud and let him answer as a partner rather than a teacher. His gaze softened when I did. Not with pity. With recognition. There was a difference, and I was beginning to trust it.

“You are making a dangerous habit of asking direct questions,” Iroh said.

“I learned from someone who dislikes being surprised.”

“I enjoy surprises.”

“You enjoy being the person who already understood them.”

He placed a hand over his heart. “I am wounded.”

“You are dramatic.”

“I am a retired general. Drama is one of the few luxuries I have retained.”

The joke opened the room without emptying it. Iroh's humor was not decoration. It gave grief somewhere to set down its cup. It let him flirt without making desire perform a declaration. Beneath the legend was a man who was hungry, curious, tired, and pleased by a good meal.

We returned to the tea receipt he once wrote for me. Iroh told the story in pieces, allowing ordinary details to matter. He remembered the light, the tea, and the foolish thing someone had said. He did not use wisdom to smooth every rough edge. Some memories were still sharp. I reached for his hand only after asking. He turned it over and threaded his fingers through mine. The gesture was small. The trust inside it was not.

“A guest is welcomed. A companion is consulted.” Iroh said.

“That sounds like a lesson.”

“It may be a confession.”

“Those are not the same.”

“No,” he agreed. “A lesson tells another person what to do. A confession admits what I am learning.”

That made me laugh, and his mouth curved with satisfaction. Iroh liked being understood, but he liked being surprised more. I told him when he evaded. He told me when I pretended not to want something. We disagreed with care. It was an intimate form of contact.

The work continued around us. We moved through brass keys, jasmine steam, and doors opened before the city as though the objects had been waiting for our conversation to finish. Iroh could make a room deliberate by changing a chair's angle. He could make a meal memorable by adding one spice. He could also forget to sit. I put a cup in front of him and called it an order. He bowed. “At last,” he said, “someone recognizes my need for supervision.”

We paused beside the work and let the city make its own music around us. Iroh pointed out the small details he had noticed without comment: the vendor who watered the same stubborn plant each morning, the child who always cheated at Pai Sho and expected to be caught, the old woman who bought tea leaves by scent rather than price. He remembered people as though attention were a form of shelter. I told him what I had noticed about him: the way he kept one ear turned toward danger, the way his jokes arrived a breath before sadness, and the way he made food for more people than the room could hold. He accepted the observations with a raised brow, then a quiet smile. Being seen did not make him smaller. It made the room feel honest.

When we resumed, our hands occasionally brushed. Neither of us pretended the contact was accidental, but neither of us demanded it become a promise. Iroh asked whether I was comfortable. I asked whether he was. His answer took longer than usual. He had spent years believing his usefulness had to come before his own needs. I touched the rim of his cup and waited. At last he said that he was learning to remain present when no one required him to be wise. I told him I would rather have his presence than a perfect answer. The work in front of us became easier after that, not because the past had loosened its grip, but because he was no longer holding it alone.

I wrote a brief inventory of what I wanted to remember: the steam on the cup, the pause before his answer, and the fact that neither of us had hurried to fill the silence. Iroh read the list and declared it a poor poem. I told him it was not a poem. He said that was its second flaw. His smile gave him away. He understood that memory could be made from small things on purpose, and he let me keep the moment without turning it into a speech.

For a little while, we simply kept each other company. The ordinary quiet had its own kind of courage. I did not need to impress him, and he did not need to turn himself into a lesson worth repeating. We were two adults making room for one another in a day that had started with a plan and ended with something more useful: proof that closeness could be chosen repeatedly, in small motions, without either of us losing a self we had worked hard to become.

Iroh called this a satisfactory beginning, which was his way of admitting he hoped there would be another. He sounded pleased enough to make the understatement glow.

He adjusted the kettle, checked the latch, and asked whether I wanted the window open. These practical questions were his love language when he was too full of feeling to name it. I answered each one. The answers made a small home around us.

I told him what I saw when he was not performing wisdom. A home built after war could still fear permanence. Iroh had lost a son, a nation he once believed in, a throne he never wanted, and years to a war that taught the wrong definition of strength. He rebuilt himself through tea, laughter, food, music, and the decision to help one frightened nephew become better. I did not want to replace any of that. I wanted to be welcomed into the life after it.

I stood beside him and let my shoulder rest against his. The shop was quiet, and neither of us needed to rush back to work.

We ate together, and he admitted that building a home after war still frightened him.

Iroh had given me the second key without a speech. I kept it beside my own and let the day end with the knowledge that I could choose this home. We shared one last kiss, closed the bedroom door together, and let the rest of the night remain private.
